content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a new DG dataset that extends the NICO dataset to have common domains that are shared across class labels.
The paper proposes two metrics to evaluate their proposed dataset compared to others that measures the amount of covariate shift (shift of $p(x)$) and concept shift (shift of $p(y|x)$).
These method-agnostic metrics provide bounds on any DG algorithm and point to the case that DG methods can only succeed if concept shift is small while covariate shift is high.
The paper then evaluates many common DG methods on the newly proposed dataset and highlights that prior datasets have significant variability with respect to model selection and hyperparameters.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
*Strengths*
- Theorem 3.3 on a lower bound of the test loss is instructive and helpful. This helps to quantify and formalize the feasibility of domain generalization for a particular domain dataset.

- The test variance shown in Table 4 is quite instructive and suggests that NICO++ is indeed quite helpful in reducing the sensitivity to hyperparameters and random seeds. (though it does raise questions about the challenge of the dataset)

- The proposed benchmark enables the ability to carefully control the domain and category distribution, which does seem important for evaluating DG methods.

*Weaknesses*
- The biggest weakness is the lack of comparison to the WILDS domain generalization benchmark suite [Koh et al., 2021]. This seems to be a major and perhaps critical flaw.  WILDS does not have the problem of only have a small number of domains and is realisitic ---two claimed advantages of the current paper.  Related to this, there is only one sentence about a comparison to NICO.  It seems that an empirical comparison to both WILDS and NICO is critical for validating the proposed work.

Koh, P. W., Sagawa, S., Marklund, H., Xie, S. M., Zhang, M., Balsubramani, A., ... & Liang, P. (2021, July). Wilds: A benchmark of in-the-wild distribution shifts. In International Conference on Machine Learning (pp. 5637-5664). PMLR.

- The second biggest weakness is the lack of clarity and paper organization. I believe this dataset offers a useful dataset to the community, but the current writing seems to be lacking in clarity and good organization. See clarity comments below.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- A small version of Figure 3 should be included in the main paper.  This is a helpful figure. In particular, it would be great to highlight interesting combinations like the camel in the water or cactus by the water.  Overall, this seems to be one of the core strengths of this dataset over prior datasets---though perhaps I missed something. A comparison to at least one other dataset that fails to have this property would also be very instructive (e.g., does PACS have this problem?).

- Is it possible that NICO++ is just an easier dataset than prior benchmark datasets?  This would explain the lower variance. If it is "easier", is this intended or not? If it is not "easier", can you give empirical evidence that it is indeed "harder" than prior bencharks?

- Why use \ell_1 distance between distributions for Mcov instead of something like Wasserstein distance? For example, suppose two distributions lie on different manifolds, then the $\ell_1$ distance will attain its max value no matter how far away these manifolds are.  However, Wasserstein distance does not suffer from this phenomena. If the manifolds are slight perturbations of each other, they will have a small distance.

- Why not take the average instead of the min and max of concept shift?  In this scenario, does train or test have specific meanings? It seems that a symmetric version would be simpler. Is it merely for the theory part?

- What is your definition of "domain label" as opposed to "class label"? Could you provide a precise definition? It seems that these could be interchangeable depending on context---e.g., if you wanted to predict water in images rather than the object. What if you flipped which labels were classes and which were domains? It seems that in your case where you have all pairwise distributions, you could easily consider this experiment---though perhaps it is infeasible in the time allowed.

*Clarity and organization*
- Theorem 3.2 should be introduced as an extension of prior theorems rather than remarking after stating the theorem. This will also lead up to the theorem better.

- You should provide the Definition 3.2 before 3.1 in the paper; otherwise, it's confusing. It also makes it sound initially like you are introducing a discrepancy definition in your metrics, but this is not the case.

- The remark after Definition 3.1 is confusing.  This should give the intuition of why both metrics are interesting and then point to the theorems that flesh them out.  The claim that they "both provide meaningful characteristics" is not supported at this point in the paper (though perhaps it is fleshed out in the theorems).  The example of a circle seems a bit arbitrary; do you just mean that if a region is entirely different class in two domains, then it would be impossible to generalize?  Or is there a reason for using a circle instead of a square?

- The caption of Figure 2 should be significantly expanded so it can stand on its own.  Right now, there is little to no explanation of the figure/illustration. I don't even understand the right side of figure 2. Where do those regions come from?  Could you draw the ftr and fte you mean?  The right also seems a bit unrealisitic but maybe I just cannot understand the figure directly.

- Tables and Figures should only be given after they are introduced.  Table 1 for example is shown before.

- "donates" -> "denotes"

- "embarrassing the convergence" - "embarraissing" seems to be the wrong word here, not sure what is meant.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed DG benchmark seems to be unique among possible benchmarks by controlling for concept and covariate shift. The theory provides some grounding for an "ideal" DG benchmark . However, the paper lacks comparison to WILDS and NICO (the paper's predecessor), which seem to be the closest related works and the clarity of writing and organization seem lacking for ICLR.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 4: The contributions are significant, and do not exist in prior works.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper addressed the problem of Domain Generalization. The authors propose a new rich benchmark dataset NICO++. They propose new metrics to evaluate the quality of datasets of DG problems and compare NICO++ with respect to these metrics to previously existing datasets.  The authors propose two metrics to quantify covariate and concept shifts: adapting a previously proposed measure for covariate shift and proposing a measure for concept shift.
The authors also propose novel generalization bounds from the perspective of data construction. They empirically demonstrate the superiority of the proposed dataset with respect to the proposed measures.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths:**

The paper introduces a novel large-scale domain generalization benchmark NICO++, which contains extensive domains and categories.

**Weaknesses and comments:**

- This paper focuses on domains different in semantics. This is an important contribution, but in real-world applications, not the only domain shift happening (e.g. Castro et al. 2020). 

- “Distribution shift within the dataset can be caused by the shift on P(X) (i.e., covariate shift) and 2The ratio of the number of categories in Animal, Plant, Vehicle and shift on P(Y|X) (i.e., concept shift)”. This is only true under the assumption of causal direction: X -> Y. Otherwise, these are not the only reasons for the distribution shift [Quiñonero-Candela, J. et al. (2009), Castro et al. (2020). So the case considered by the authors is important, it is good to keep in mind that it is not only one and this sentence gives a wrong impression.
- [About Remark on page 4.] As mentioned above, this definition of concept shift only makes sense in a causal direction [Quiñonero-Candela, J. et al. (2008)]. P(Y | X) can still change without a change in the labeling rule if the data-generating process was anti-causal: Y -> X.
- “When there is a strong inconsistency between labeling rules on training and test data, the classification loss instructing biased connections between visual features and concepts is misleading for generalization to test data.” They certainly are. But this is not the only reason for the models not being able to generalize well. Significant covariate shift is also not only reason. Since the authors consider a causal direction, then the model should be able to generalize well if the features selected by the model were causal [Arjovsky et al. 2019]. 
- In Theorem 3.3, if we assume that no “mislabeling” happened (no concept shift), then the lower bound becomes meaningless? 
- In section 3.3: “For the concept shift, we estimate ftr and fte with models that fit the source set and target set, respectively. Specifically, we learn two models on the source and target set of a given dataset, respectively, with the objective of category recognition and each of them on both source and target data.” How do you know that these two random models will truly evaluate concept shift and not just spurious correlations picked up by the models in each domain? Given that, I am concerned that the results in Table 1 should be truly interpreted as a measure of concept shift.
- I am confused by section 4.1. If I understood correctly, the authors propose to use evaluation metrics on test domain, when in the paper of Gulrajani&Lopez-Paz it was discussed that this strategy should be avoided. Also, to my knowledge, the strategy of leave-one-out is used for hyperparameter tuning, and after the best model is retrained on all source domains and can be evaluated on test domains under ant appropriate metrics. So the comment about std is not clear to me either. It looks like here hyperparameter tuning and final testing were confused. But taking this apart, metrics in 5 do look sensible, but not like a breakthrough.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The dataset proposed by the author is certainly novel and interesting. The rest of the paper is not clear though, as for example, strong conclusions lead to the evaluation section. The whole motivation is built on the superiority of the dataset with respect to introduced metrics, but the jump from bound theorems to empirical evaluation is not clear.
content.summary_of_the_review: I recognize the contribution of this paper by introducing a new reach dataset, which would allow us to push research on domain generalization forward, but I am not convinced by the theoretical part and by empirical evaluation. Many statements are unclear or provide a one-sided view of the problem without a clear disclaimer about it. The experimental section is not convincing because of the choice of metrics and exactly very biased consideration of what the problem “could have been”. The jump from upper/lower bounds to the use of two random models to estimate them and use as a measure of comparison for completely different datasets is not clear to me at all.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper introduces a new dataset called NICO++, which is intended to be used for benchmarking domain generalization methods on both the conventional DG problem setting and a new setting called flexible DG proposed in the submission. In addition to introducing this new dataset, the paper also includes theoretical analysis into the domain adaptation problem, and an empirical investigation into how well existing DG methods work on this new dataset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths
* The proposed dataset seems to be quite large, but still not so large as to preclude its use in academic labs.
* The new flexible DG setting seems like it may be a useful problem formalisation.
* The performance evaluation of many existing approaches on this new dataset provides a useful indication for both how well one should expect novel methods to perform, and also as another point of comparison for the general applicability of the existing methods.

### Weaknesses
* Clarity and details are lacking in places This is particularly troublesome in the definition of the flexible DG setting, which has quite an uninformative name and is not well described anywhere. However, it also smaller details such as where the data has actually been collected from, how the annotators were recruited, what instructions they were given, and what kinds of biases or limitations the collection strategy is likely to have.
* The theoretical analysis is for domain adaptation, not domain generalisation. I do not understand how it is relevant to the problem of domain generalisation when the quantities that appear in the upper bounds cannot be estimated reliably. Including this unrelated material in the paper makes it harder to follow.
* The justification of the dataset seems to be that it is easier than other DG benchmarks. If it is easy to solve then what the point of using it? I.e., what novel insights can this proposed dataset give us?
* Most of the comparison is with smaller DG datasets such as PACS and VLCS. How does it compare to larger and more recent DG benchmarks like WILDS?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I think many of the main issues stem from a lack of details, which impinges on clarity and will harm reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: Given the weaknesses highlights above I cannot recommend acceptance.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
